subject: Microbiology
vignette: A 48-year-old man presents with 2 days of fever, confusion, and a fluent aphasia. He has no focal motor deficits. Brain MRI shows hyperintensity in the medial temporal lobes and insula. CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and a normal glucose. Herpes simplex virus-1 PCR of the CSF is positive.
question: Which of the following best explains why this particular syndrome is attributed to HSV-1?

options.text: HSV-1 is the most common cause of sporadic encephalitis, characteristically affecting the temporal lobes with altered mental status, seizures, or aphasia
HSV-1 is an enveloped DNA virus that acquires its envelope from the nuclear membrane, which explains its tropism
HSV-1 latency in mononuclear cells leads to intranuclear owl's eye inclusions in neurons
HSV-1 is the agent of the classic aseptic meningitis syndrome more often than HSV-2
HSV-1 reactivates from the sacral ganglia and spreads along sacral nerve roots to the temporal lobe

explanation_correct: HSV-1 is the most common cause of sporadic encephalitis, classically presenting with altered mental status, seizures, and aphasia and targeting the temporal lobes. It is transmitted by respiratory secretions and saliva and remains latent in the trigeminal ganglia, which is why reactivation can seed the anterior and middle cranial fossa. CSF PCR is the test of choice for herpes encephalitis.

explanation_incorrect.B: Herpesviruses do acquire enveloped from the nuclear membrane, but that is true of all herpesviruses and does not explain temporal lobe tropism.
explanation_incorrect.C: Owl's eye intranuclear inclusions are the hallmark of cytomegalovirus; HSV and VZV show Cowdry A inclusions instead.
explanation_incorrect.D: Viral meningitis is more common with HSV-2 than HSV-1; HSV-1 is distinguished by encephalitis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Sacral ganglia latency belongs to HSV-2, which causes herpes genitalis, neonatal herpes, and viral meningitis.

educationalObjective: HSV-1 is the most common cause of sporadic encephalitis, with temporal lobe involvement and altered mental status, seizures, or aphasia; CSF PCR is diagnostic.

subject: Microbiology
vignette: A 26-year-old woman presents with a single 3-mm erythematous swelling of the distal index finger that appeared 2 days after she bit her nail carelessly; she is a dental hygienist. It is exquisitely tender and has a cluster of small vesicles that later coalesced into a coalescing crust.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis and its agent?

options.text: Herpetic whitlow from HSV-1 or HSV-2

explanation_correct: Herpetic whitlow is a painful vesicular lesion of the distal finger caused by inoculation of HSV-1 (or HSV-2) into broken skin, classically in healthcare workers such as dental hygienists who are exposed to oral secretions. It is one of the recognized HSV-1 clinical syndromes in First Aid, alongside gingivostomatitis, keratoconjunctivitis, herpes labialis, temporal lobe encephalitis, esophagitis, and erythema multiforme.

explanation_incorrect.A: Bacterial paronychia also affects the nail fold, but the clustered clear vesicles and occupational exposure to saliva in the absence of purulent drainage point to a viral etiology.
explanation_incorrect.B: Herpangina is an oropharyngeal disease with mouth blisters and fever caused by coxsackievirus, not a digital lesion.
explanation_incorrect.C: Gianotti-Crosti is a papular acrodermatitis associated with viral infection, not a localized vesicle of the fingertip.
explanation_incorrect.E: Erythema multiforme is a targetoid cutaneous eruption that can follow HSV, but it is a generalized rash rather than a localized vesicular finger lesion.

educationalObjective: Herpetic whitlow is an HSV-1 or HSV-2 infection of the finger acquired by inoculation of broken skin, classically in dental or healthcare workers.

subject: Microbiology
vignette: A 22-year-old woman presents with a painful labial vesicle that ruptured and crusted over 3 days. She reports previous similar episodes triggered by sun exposure. The clinician considers the classic bedside test for a viral vesicle.
question: A Tzanck smear of an opened vesicle in this patient would most likely show which of the following?

options.text: Multinucleated giant cells with Cowdry A intranuclear inclusions
Cells with owl's eye intranuclear inclusions
Negri bodies in the cytoplasm of neurons

explanation_correct: The Tzanck test is a smear of an opened skin vesicle that detects multinucleated giant cells, which are commonly seen with HSV-1, HSV-2, and VZV. Intranuclear eosinophilic Cowdry A inclusions are also seen in these infections. The test is now outdated: PCR of skin lesions is the diagnostic test of choice.

explanation_incorrect.B: Owl's eye inclusions are characteristic of cytomegalovirus-infected cells, not of the multinucleated giant cells of HSV or VZV.
explanation_incorrect.C: Negri bodies are cytoplasmic inclusions of rabies virus found in Purkinje cells of the cerebellum and hippocampal neurons.
explanation_incorrect.D: Koilocytes with perinuclear halos are the cytopathic effect of human papillomavirus on squamous epithelium.
explanation_incorrect.E: Molluscum bodies are intracytoplasmic inclusions in keratinocytes of molluscum contagiosum, a poxvirus lesion.

educationalObjective: A Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells (plus Cowdry A inclusions) in HSV-1, HSV-2, and VZV lesions, although PCR of the lesion is now the test of choice.
